title: Automated versus Manual Impaction in Total Hip Arthroplasty: Effects on the Surgeon’s Ergonomics
summary:
Work-related musculoskeletal disorders are a common occupational health risk in total hip arthroplasty (THA), affecting approximately two-thirds of surgeons. Automated impaction systems, such as the DePuy Synthes KINCISE™, replace manual impaction techniques during these procedures. Manual impactions are associated with poor ergonomic postures, high peak forces, and a high number of repetitive movements, potentially contributing to increased physical strain and muscle fatigue among surgeons.
Despite promising results from previous studies, the actual ergonomic benefits of automated impaction systems have not yet been objectively demonstrated. This is primarily due to the lack of intraoperative measurements in real patients and the limited number of surgeons investigated.
To objectively assess the differences between manual and automated impaction techniques, four surgeons will be examined over six operating days each. Three days will involve manual impaction and three days automated impaction. Four total hip arthroplasties will be performed per day, with measurements taken during the first and fourth procedures.

interventions.name: Intervention grout: Automated impaction. Four surgeons (males and females) execute the automated impaction during surgeries on 3 days each. Every first and fourth surgery gets measured
Control group: Manual impaction. Four surgeons (males and females) execute the manual impaction during surgeries on 3 days each. Every first and fourth surgery gets measured

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Board-certified surgeons and experienced residents with at least 50 independently performed total hip arthroplasty (THA) procedures
- Proficiency in both impaction techniques (manual and automated)
- Provision of informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
- Musculoskeletal injuries or pain syndromes affecting the upper extremities or spine within the past three months
- Skin lesions at the intended electrode placement sites
- Lack of capacity to provide informed consent
